messages.subject: Posterior marginal density looks wired, what parameter should I tune?
parts:
Sorry for keep asking questions in this email list. I just started using INLA and may not ask good questions.
I was checking the posterior densities of the fixed effect produced from the following model. The intercept and one other fixed effect have wired density plot. What are the possible reasons causing that?



# i: represent county i
# j: represent the j-th patient in county i
Y ~ Weibull(alpha, lambda_{ij})
log(lambda_{ij}) = alpha_i + stage_{ij} + age_{ij} + b_i + e_{ij}
where:
alpha_i: intercept
stage_{ij}: the cancer stage of the patient ij, I created 3 dummies variables s1, s2 and s3 in the following code.
age_{ij}: the age of the patient, put in 12 categories, with values 1,2,...,12
b_i: I want to use BYM2 with PC priors
e_{ij}: lack of fit (error) at individual level



Here is my model:
dat = list(
  y=y,
  s1 = Xs[,1],
  s2 = Xs[,2],
  s3 = Xs[,3],
  unfac_age=t_data$age_group,
  ID1 = 1:length(y),
  ID2 = t_data$county
)
formula=inla.surv(y,Delta_vec)~s1+s2+s3 +
  f(unfac_age, model="rw2", hyper = list(prec = list(prior="loggamma", param=c(1,0.005))))+
  f(ID1, model="iid", hyper = list(prec = list(prior="loggamma", param=c(1,0.005))))+
  f(ID2, model="bym", graph=g_MO, scale.model=TRUE,initial = 1,
    hyper=list(
      prec.unstruct=list(prior="loggamma", param=c(1,0.001)),
      prec.spatial=list(prior="loggamma", param=c(1,0.001))
    ))
model=inla(formula, family ="weibullsurv", data=dat,verbose = TRUE,
           control.fixed=list(prec.intercept=0.001,
                              prec=list(s1=0.001, s2=0.001, s3=0.001)),
           control.compute=list(dic=TRUE))

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Posterior marginal density looks wired, what parameter should I tune?
parts: The situation comes up with the following fitting where I only preset the precision of the intercept to be 0.01 (to avoid numerical singular warning):
model=inla(formula, family ="weibullsurv", data=dat,verbose = TRUE,

control.fixed=list(prec.intercept=0.01),
           control.compute=list(dic=TRUE))
I am rerunning the above model with verbose=False so that I can attach the log file.

I was suspecting if the precision of other fixed effect will cause an issue. So instead, I ran the 2nd model below having larger variance which gave me no problem:

model=inla(formula, family ="weibullsurv", data=dat,verbose = TRUE,
           control.fixed=list(prec.intercept=0.001,
                              prec=list(s1=0.001, s2=0.001, s3=0.001)),
           control.compute=list(dic=TRUE))

Is that the reason for wired posterior density?

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Posterior marginal density looks wired, what parameter should I tune?
parts:
My best guess (which is admittedly less experienced than Haavards best guess!) is that the integration over the hyper-parameters is not very nice (because of a strange posterior, like a bad fit). This could result in "two different intercepts".

For low variance, you will see these two different intercepts as different bumps, but with a larger variance you may not see them, since they overlap so much. This does not mean that your issue is solved, just that you cannot detect it.

I can usually check for this issue by looking at the logfile :)


Haakon

messages.author: 9940b4fcc153c7d7
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Posterior marginal density looks wired, what parameter should I tune?
parts:
Observations from the log file

"Mode not sufficient accurate; switch to a stupid local search strategy.
...
"

This means that the estimation procedure is slightly unstable. As in, you can get a bit different results when re-running, or using different initial values.

Later in the log it seems like the posterior approximation is "bad but not useless". I would suggest re-running with initial values being 
theta= 0.104639 4.729527 0.561453 6.988732 4.332334

I think your results will change a bit. If you want, I can check the logfile afterwards.

My best guess (from the logfile) is that the posterior / likelihood-on-your-data, is badly behaved for the weibull survival alpha. I do not know much about survival analysis, so I cannot tell you why this would happen.

PS. Another idea would be to fix survival-alpha and see of the rest of the model is well behaved.

Kind regards,
Haakon
